title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
summary: A usually noisy class must work in total silence during a reading exercise, and one boy who struggles to focus discovers he actually reads better in a quiet room.
poll: Classrooms should always be lively, with lots of talking and discussion, instead of quiet.

versions.title: A Quiet Day
versions.text:
Faisal's class is noisy. Kids talk a lot. Kids laugh a lot. Chairs scrape the floor. Pens tap on desks. It is hard to hear.

One day, the teacher has a plan. "We will read in silence," she says. "No talk at all."

The class is sad. Omar says, "That will be dull!" Faisal is worried too. He has a hard time with focus. He thinks quiet will make it worse.

But then it happens. The room goes quiet. Faisal reads fast. He gets each word. He ends his book first!

Faisal is shocked. He tells the teacher, "I read best in quiet!"

She smiles. "What a fine thing to discover," she says. "Some kids need quiet. Thanks for this news."

After that, the class has quiet time each week. Kids like it. Faisal does his best work then.

versions.title: A Quiet Day
versions.text:
Faisal's room is noisy most days. Kids talk and laugh at once. Chairs scrape the floor. Pens tap on desks a lot. It is hard to hear.

One day, the teacher has a plan. "Today we read in silence," she tells the class. "No talk, no sound at all."

The class groans out loud. Omar says, "That will be so dull!" Faisal feels worried too. He finds it hard to focus. He thinks quiet will make it worse.

But then an odd thing happens. The room goes quiet. Faisal reads much faster now. He gets each word right. He ends his book first!

Faisal feels very glad. He tells the teacher, "I read best when quiet!"

She smiles at him. "What a fine thing to discover," she says. "Kids need different things."

After that day, the class has quiet time each week. Many kids say they like it. Faisal does his best work then.

versions.title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
versions.text:
Faisal's room is almost always noisy. Kids talk and laugh at the same time. Chairs scrape the floor, and pens tap on desks. It is often hard to hear the teacher.

One morning, the teacher shares a new plan. "Today we will read in total silence," she tells the class. "No talking, no sound at all."

The class groans at this. Omar raises his hand and says, "That sounds so dull!" Faisal feels worried too, but for a different reason. He finds it hard to focus when he reads.

But an odd thing happens once the room goes quiet. Faisal finds he reads much faster than before. He gets every word without a second look. He finishes his book before his classmates!

Faisal feels amazed by this. After class, he tells the teacher, "I read better when it is quiet!"

The teacher smiles warmly. "That is a great thing to discover about yourself," she says. "Different readers need different things."

From that day on, the class has quiet time each week. Many kids say they like it too, and Faisal does his best work then.

versions.title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
versions.text:
Faisal's room is almost always noisy. Every day, kids talk and laugh at the same time, chairs scrape the floor, and pens tap on desks without stopping. It is often hard to hear the teacher over all the noise.

One morning, the teacher shares a new plan. "Today we will read in complete silence," she tells the class. "No talk, no sound at all, from start to finish."

The class groans at this, clearly unhappy. Omar raises his hand and says, "That sounds really dull!" Faisal feels worried too, though for a different reason: he finds it hard to focus when he reads.

But an odd thing happens once the room finally goes quiet. Faisal finds he is reading much faster than before, with far less work. He gets every word, with no need to look twice. He finishes his whole book before any of his classmates!

Faisal feels truly amazed by this. After class, he walks up to the teacher and says, "I read much better when it is quiet!"

The teacher smiles warmly at him. "That is a great thing to discover about yourself," she replies. "Different readers need different things in order to focus well."

From that day on, the class has quiet time every week. Many kids say they enjoy the silence too, and Faisal does his best work during those calm, quiet minutes.

versions.title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
versions.text:
Every day, Faisal's room buzzed with noise. Students talked over one another. Chairs scraped the floor. Pencils tapped out restless beats on desks. It was part of the daily routine. It was so normal that hardly anyone noticed it. Hardly anyone, that is, except Faisal. He quietly struggled to concentrate through all of it.

One morning, the teacher introduced a plan. It broke that routine completely. "Today," she announced, "we will spend reading time in complete silence. No talking, no whispering, not even a whisper of sound." Groans spread through the room. Omar complained loudly that the plan sounded unbearably dull. Faisal felt reluctant too, for a reason nobody else shared. He assumed that losing every distraction would make his reading worse.

What happened next surprised him completely. In the hush of the silent room, Faisal read faster and more clearly than ever before. Each sentence made sense right away. There was no need to reread confusing lines. He finished his book before a single classmate had turned the final page.

Stunned by what had happened, Faisal approached the teacher once the period ended. "I think I actually read better in silence," he told her, still sounding amazed.

The teacher's face softened into a proud smile. "That's an important thing to realize about yourself," she said. "Readers concentrate in different ways." From then on, quiet reading time became part of the class routine. Several classmates admitted that the silence helped them concentrate too.

Omar complained loudly that the exercise sounded unbearably dull. versions.title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
versions.text:
Every day, without exception, Faisal's room buzzed with constant, cheerful noise, the kind that most students had long since stopped noticing. They talked over one another at every opportunity, chairs scraped loudly against the floor, and pencils tapped out restless rhythms that rarely paused for long, forming an unquestioned part of the daily routine. Unquestioned, that is, except by Faisal, who quietly struggled to concentrate through all of it without ever truly understanding why reading felt so unusually difficult for him compared with his classmates.

One morning, the teacher introduced a plan that broke that familiar routine entirely. She announced calmly that the class would spend the reading period fully immersed in complete silence, with no talking, no whispering, and not even the faintest whisper of sound. This prospect drew a chorus of groans and several disbelieving glances from around the room. Omar complained loudly that the exercise sounded unbearably dull, while Faisal felt reluctant as well, though for a very different reason than his classmates: he simply assumed that removing every familiar distraction would make his usual struggles even worse than they already were.

What happened next surprised him completely. Once immersed in the hush of the silent room, Faisal read faster and more clearly than he ever had in the past, understanding each sentence the very first time through, almost as though the words themselves had suddenly become easier to understand than ever before. He finished his entire book before a single classmate had even turned to the final page, a result that astonished even him and left him staring at his own notebook in quiet disbelief.

Stunned by this small revelation about himself, Faisal approached the teacher the moment the period ended. He admitted, his voice still carrying a trace of amazement, that he read much better in complete silence, as though describing someone else's experience entirely.

The teacher's expression softened into a proud, understanding smile. She explained that this was an important insight for him to acknowledge about himself, since every reader needs to concentrate in a slightly different way, and now he finally understood exactly what his own way required in order to be productive. From that day forward, quiet reading time became a regular, welcomed part of the classroom routine that students began to look forward to rather than dread. Several classmates eventually acknowledged that the silence helped their own concentration as well.

They talked over one another at every opportunity, chairs scraped loudly against the floor, and pencils tapped out restless rhythms that rarely paused for long. Unquestioned, that is, by everyone except Faisal, who quietly struggled to concentrate through all of it without ever truly understanding why reading felt so unusually difficult for him compared with classmates who seemed to manage perfectly well amid the constant commotion.

One morning, the teacher introduced a plan that broke that familiar routine entirely. She announced calmly that the class would spend the reading period fully immersed in complete silence, with no talking, no whispering, and not even the faintest whisper of sound. This prospect drew a chorus of groans and several disbelieving glances from classmates who could not imagine an hour without conversation. Omar complained loudly that the exercise sounded unbearably dull, while Faisal felt reluctant as well, though for a very different reason than his classmates: he simply assumed that removing every familiar distraction would make his usual struggles even worse than they already were.

What happened next surprised him completely. Once immersed in the hush of the silent room, Faisal read faster and more clearly than he ever had in the past, understanding each sentence the very first time through, almost as though the words themselves had suddenly become easier to understand than ever before. He finished his entire book before a single classmate had even turned to the final page, a result that astonished even him and left him staring at his own notebook in quiet disbelief, uncertain how a single change in the room could matter so much.

Stunned by this small revelation about himself, Faisal approached the teacher the moment the period ended. He admitted, his voice still carrying a trace of amazement, that he read much better in complete silence, as though describing someone else's experience entirely.

The teacher's expression softened into a proud, understanding smile. She explained that this was an important insight for him to acknowledge about himself, since every reader needs to concentrate in a slightly different way, and now he finally understood exactly what his own way required in order to be productive. From that day forward, quiet reading time became a regular, welcomed part of the classroom routine that students began to look forward to rather than dread. Several classmates eventually acknowledged that the silence helped their own concentration as well, making it quickly the most productive, and most genuinely popular, part of the week.

versions.title: The Day the Classroom Went Quiet
versions.text:
Faisal's classroom buzzed every single day with constant, cheerful noise that most students had long since stopped noticing, since it had simply become the unexamined background hum of their shared routine: students talked over one another at every opportunity, chairs scraped loudly against the floor, and pencils tapped out restless rhythms that rarely paused for long, an unquestioned normalcy that nevertheless left Faisal quietly struggling to concentrate through all of it, session after session, without ever truly understanding why reading felt so unusually difficult for him compared with classmates who appeared to manage perfectly well amid the constant commotion surrounding them.

One morning, the teacher introduced a plan that broke that familiar routine entirely, announcing calmly that the class would spend the reading period fully immersed in complete silence, with no talking, no whispering, and not even the faintest whisper of sound, a prospect that drew both a chorus of groans and several disbelieving glances from classmates who could not imagine an entire hour devoid of conversation; Omar complained loudly that the exercise sounded unbearably dull, while Faisal felt reluctant for an entirely different reason, since he simply assumed that removing every familiar distraction would somehow make his usual struggles even worse than they already were, having never once experienced reading without some kind of background noise against which to measure himself.

What happened next surprised him completely: once immersed in the hush of the silent classroom, Faisal read faster and more clearly than he ever had in the past, understanding each sentence the very first time through, almost as though the words themselves had suddenly become easier to understand than ever before, and he finished his entire book before a single classmate had even turned to the final page, a result that astonished even him and left him staring at his own notebook in quiet disbelief, uncertain how a single change to the room could matter so profoundly to his own performance.

Stunned by this small revelation about himself, Faisal approached the teacher the moment the period ended and admitted, his voice still carrying a trace of amazement, that he actually read much better in complete silence, as though describing someone else's experience entirely rather than his own; the teacher's expression softened into a proud, understanding smile as she explained that this was an important insight for him to acknowledge about himself, since every reader needs to concentrate in a slightly different way, and some students barely notice background noise at all while others find that the smallest sound pulls their attention from the page, neither way of reading being better than the other, but each requiring a somewhat different environment in order to be productive.

From that day forward, quiet reading time became a regular, welcomed part of the classroom routine that students began to look forward to rather than dread, and several classmates eventually acknowledged that the silence helped their own concentration as well, transforming what had begun as an unusual, unwanted exercise into the most productive, and most genuinely popular, part of nearly everyone's week — a small, unexpected lesson in how profoundly the environment surrounding a reader can shape that reader's performance, and in how a student who seems to struggle in one setting might simply be waiting for the right conditions in which to succeed.

A strict teacher who never lets students talk

wrong.C: Faisal's concern is about his own reading, not about disliking rules.
wrong.D: The story does not say Faisal wants to talk during reading.

questions.stem: According to the story, what does the teacher say every reader needs?
options: To complete every reading assignment while working in a group
To read the books that the teacher picks for them
To avoid quiet rooms because they feel too lonely for most readers
To concentrate in whatever way works best for that reader
questions.why: The teacher tells Faisal that every reader needs to concentrate in a slightly different way.

wrong.A: The story does not say reading must always be done in groups.
wrong.B: The story does not mention the teacher choosing books for students.
wrong.C: Faisal's experience shows quiet rooms can help, not hurt, some readers.

questions.stem: Which event happens immediately after Faisal finishes his book first?
options: The classroom immediately becomes loud and noisy again, just as before
Faisal is stunned and approaches the teacher once the period ends
Omar apologizes to Faisal for complaining earlier that morning
The quiet reading time begins before Faisal even finishes reading
questions.why: After finishing first and feeling stunned, Faisal walks up to the teacher once the reading period ends to tell her what happened.

wrong.A: The classroom stays quiet until the period ends, not right away.
wrong.C: The story does not describe Omar apologizing.
wrong.D: The quiet reading time begins before Faisal finishes, not after.

questions.stem: Why does Faisal assume that silence will make his reading worse before trying it?
options: Because the teacher had specifically and repeatedly told him that total silence would be extremely difficult for him
Because Omar warned him earlier that morning about the plan
Because he has struggled to focus before and does not yet realize that noise, not silence, was the real problem
Because he generally dislikes reading
questions.why: Faisal has often struggled with reading in his noisy classroom, so he naturally assumes silence, not noise, is the cause of his trouble.

wrong.A: The teacher does not tell Faisal that silence will be difficult.
wrong.B: The story does not say Omar warns Faisal about anything.
wrong.D: Faisal enjoys reading once the room is quiet, so he does not dislike reading itself.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about why some of Faisal's classmates also enjoy the silent reading time?
options: They may also concentrate better without background noise, even though they had not noticed this before
They want to copy whatever Faisal does in class each day, even when it does not help them with their schoolwork
They are bored of talking to each other during the school day
The teacher makes them say in front of the class that they enjoy it
questions.why: Like Faisal, other classmates may concentrate better in silence without ever having noticed it before this exercise.

wrong.B: The story does not say classmates are only copying Faisal.
wrong.C: The story does not suggest classmates are simply bored of talking.
wrong.D: The story does not say the teacher forces anyone to say this.

questions.stem: In the story, the word reluctant means —
options: excited and eager to begin something new
confused and lost about what to do next
angry and shouting loudly at others
unwilling or hesitant to do something
questions.why: Faisal feels reluctant, meaning unwilling, because he expects silence to hurt his reading.

wrong.A: Reluctant is close to the opposite of excited and eager.
wrong.B: Reluctant describes unwillingness, not confusion.
wrong.C: Faisal feels worried quietly, not angry or loud.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the story?
options: By comparing two different schools located in two separate and distant cities
By describing the noisy routine, then the silent plan, then Faisal's discovery
By listing numbered steps for building a quiet reading room
By describing a full year of school activities, day by day, from the very start to the very end of the term
questions.why: The story first describes the usual noisy routine, then the new silent plan, and then Faisal's surprising discovery and its lasting effect.

wrong.A: The story does not compare two different schools.
wrong.C: The story is not a list of building steps.
wrong.D: The story covers one day and its lasting effect, not a full year.

MID.prompt: Explain how Faisal's experience during the silent reading time changed what he understood about himself. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained what Faisal learned about himself.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Before the silent reading time, Faisal assumed that he simply struggled to read well, and he feared that removing the usual classroom noise would make things worse. Once the room went quiet, however, he read faster and understood every sentence the first time, finishing before any of his classmates. This experience helped Faisal realize that noise, not his own ability, had been the real distraction all along, and he shared this discovery with his teacher.

keyWords.definition: to involve yourself completely in an activity or situation
keyWords.example: She immersed herself in the new novel all weekend.

keyWords.definition: able to do or make a useful amount of work
keyWords.example: A good night's sleep makes most people more productive the next day.

keyWords.definition: a clear understanding of something, often gained suddenly
keyWords.example: Her coach's advice gave her new insight into improving her swing.

keyWords.definition: to accept or admit that something is true
keyWords.example: He finally acknowledged that he had made a mistake.

keyWords.definition: a surprising fact that becomes known, often suddenly
keyWords.example: Learning that she could paint so well was a wonderful revelation for her.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: A silent classroom is more enjoyable than a noisy one for absolutely every student in the school
A student's apparent struggle may stem from his surroundings rather than his ability, and discovering this benefits the whole class
Teachers should not allow talking in their classrooms, even when students need to ask a question
Omar's loud complaints are ultimately proven correct by the end of the passage, and the teacher admits her mistake to the class
questions.why: Faisal's struggle turns out to be caused by noise, not a lack of ability, and recognizing this helps the whole class rethink how students concentrate.

wrong.A: The passage suggests needs differ between students, not that silence is best for everyone.
wrong.C: The passage does not argue that talking should always be banned.
wrong.D: Omar expects the exercise to be dull, but the passage does not focus on proving him right.

questions.stem: What had Faisal always assumed about reading in silence, before he actually experienced it himself?
options: That removing his familiar distractions would make his usual struggles worse
That the teacher would never assign such an unusual reading exercise in his class
That his classmates would also struggle more than they already did
That silence would make the classroom feel unpleasantly cold
questions.why: In the passage, Faisal assumed removing every familiar distraction would make his usual reading struggles even worse.

wrong.B: The passage does not say Faisal doubted the teacher would assign the exercise.
wrong.C: Faisal's assumption is about his own reading, not his classmates'.
wrong.D: The passage never mentions the temperature of the room.

questions.stem: According to the teacher, what must a reader acknowledge in order to become more productive?
options: That reading quickly matters more than understanding the material
That group work produces better results than reading alone
An understanding of their own particular way of concentrating
That every classroom should be silent
questions.why: The teacher explains that understanding how you personally concentrate best is what allows a reader to become productive.

wrong.A: The passage emphasizes understanding, not just speed.
wrong.B: The passage does not compare group work with reading alone.
wrong.D: The teacher says different readers need different things, not constant silence for everyone.

questions.stem: What does Faisal's surprise at his own performance suggest about how he previously viewed his reading difficulties?
options: He likely believed his difficulty was simply part of who he was, rather than caused by noise around him
He had never once tried to read any book before that particular morning in his life, so he was surprised
He secretly suspected silence would help him, but he was too shy to tell anyone
He believed his classmates were deliberately distracting him on purpose to make him fail the test
questions.why: His astonishment suggests he had accepted his struggle as a personal limitation, not realizing the noisy environment was the real cause.

wrong.B: The passage implies Faisal reads regularly, just with difficulty.
wrong.C: His amazement shows he did not expect this outcome.
wrong.D: The passage does not suggest classmates distracted him on purpose.

questions.stem: What does the lesson learned by the whole class, mentioned near the end of the passage, suggest about judging students who seem to struggle?
options: Such students are simply less capable than their classmates
A struggling student might need different conditions, not less ability
Such students should be separated into their own classroom
Struggling students usually improve only through extra homework and longer days
questions.why: The passage suggests that a student's struggle may come from the environment rather than from a lack of ability, so judgments should consider conditions.

wrong.A: Faisal's case shows ability was not the issue; the environment was.
wrong.C: The passage does not suggest separating struggling students.
wrong.D: The passage never mentions homework as the solution.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word acknowledge most nearly means —
options: to forget about something important or someone
to argue strongly against an idea
to ignore something on purpose
to accept or admit that something is true
questions.why: The teacher and the classmates acknowledge, or admit, that silence genuinely helps their concentration.

wrong.A: Acknowledge means to accept, which is close to the opposite of forgetting.
wrong.B: Acknowledging something means accepting it, not arguing against it.
wrong.C: Acknowledge means paying attention to something, not ignoring it.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the teacher's explanation that neither way of reading is better than the other?
options: To emphasize that different learning needs are equally valid, not a flaw
To argue that silent reading should be required in every classroom
To suggest that noisy classrooms are secretly more effective than quiet ones
To explain why Omar's opinion about the exercise was mistaken
questions.why: This explanation reframes differing concentration needs as natural and equally valid, rather than as a weakness in some students.

wrong.B: The teacher says different readers need different things, not that silence should always be required.
wrong.C: The passage does not claim noisy classrooms are more effective.
wrong.D: The explanation is about concentration styles in general, not about judging Omar's opinion.

questions.stem: How does Faisal's assumption before the silent exercise compare with Omar's expectation of it?
options: Omar and Faisal both expected the exercise to help their reading in exactly the same way, and both were right
Omar secretly agreed with Faisal from the very beginning of the story, and so they never argued about the exercise
Faisal expected the exercise to be boring, exactly like Omar did, but both of them enjoyed it greatly in the end
Omar expected the exercise to be dull, while Faisal feared it would hurt his reading, and both turned out to be mistaken
questions.why: Omar predicted boredom while Faisal predicted that silence would worsen his reading struggles; the passage shows neither prediction came true.

wrong.A: Omar and Faisal have different, not matching, worries about the exercise.
wrong.B: The passage gives no sign that Omar secretly agreed with Faisal.
wrong.C: Faisal's worry is about his reading ability, not about boredom.

HIGH.prompt: Some people think classrooms should always be lively and full of discussion, while others think quiet time helps students learn best. Using evidence from the passage, argue for the kind of classroom environment you think helps students read and learn best.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the question.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the passage.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe classrooms benefit most from offering both lively discussion and quiet time, rather than choosing only one. The passage shows that Faisal, who struggled during the usual noisy routine, became far more productive once the room was immersed in silence, finishing his book before any classmate. At the same time, several of his classmates also acknowledged that the silence helped their own concentration, suggesting that quiet time serves many students well. Someone might argue that constant silence would make a classroom feel lifeless, but the passage never claims silence must replace discussion entirely; it simply shows that offering quiet time alongside normal class activities lets students like Faisal discover what truly helps them succeed.

LOW.stem: What does Omar say about the silent reading plan?
options: That it will be dull
That it will be fun
That it will be too short
That it will be easy
LOW.why: In the story, Omar says the plan will be dull.

wrong.B: Omar does not think it will be fun.
wrong.C: He does not say anything about length.
wrong.D: He does not say it will be easy.

LOW.stem: What do the chairs do in the noisy classroom?
options: They break on the floor
They fall over often
They scrape the floor
They move by themselves
LOW.why: The text says, "Chairs scrape the floor."

wrong.A: The chairs do not break.
wrong.B: The chairs do not fall over.
wrong.D: The chairs do not move on their own.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does "focus" mean?
options: To run very fast outside
To think about one thing
To tell a very funny joke
To clean the whole room
LOW.why: Faisal has a hard time with focus in the noise, but in quiet he reads each word well.

wrong.A: Running does not fit reading in class.
wrong.C: Jokes do not fit the sentence.
wrong.D: Cleaning does not fit the sentence.

LOW.stem: Why does the class have quiet time each week after that day?
options: The teacher is tired of all the noise
The kids want to sleep at school
The class has no more books
Some kids work best in quiet
LOW.why: Faisal reads best in quiet and does his best work then, so the class keeps quiet time.

wrong.A: The text does not say the teacher is tired.
wrong.B: The kids read in quiet time, they do not sleep.
wrong.C: The kids read books during quiet time.

MID.stem: What did Faisal not need to do while reading in the silent room?
options: Turn the pages
Read the book
Reread confusing lines
Sit in his chair
MID.why: The text says there was no need to reread confusing lines.

wrong.A: He still turned pages and finished his book.
wrong.B: He read the whole book.
wrong.D: The text does not say he left his chair.

MID.stem: In the story, the word "routine" means —
options: something done the same way each day
a surprise that happens once
a loud game with friends
a hard test at the end of the year
MID.why: The noise was part of the daily routine, so routine means what happens the same way each day.

wrong.B: The noise happened every day, not once.
wrong.C: A routine is not a game.
wrong.D: A routine is not a test.

MID.stem: Why did Omar complain about the silent reading plan?
options: He had lost his book
He wanted to talk to Faisal
He was afraid of the teacher
He thought the plan sounded dull
MID.why: Omar complained that the plan sounded unbearably dull.

wrong.A: The text does not say he lost his book.
wrong.B: He did not say he wanted to talk to Faisal.
wrong.C: He complained loudly, so he was not afraid.

MID.stem: Why does the author say that hardly anyone noticed the noise, except Faisal?
options: To show that Faisal liked all the noise
To show the noise bothered Faisal most
To show the room was really quiet then
To show that Faisal was the teacher
MID.why: Faisal quietly struggled to concentrate through the noise, so it affected him more than others.

wrong.A: He struggled with the noise, so he did not like it.
wrong.C: The room was noisy.
wrong.D: Faisal is a student.

HIGH.stem: How did Faisal's reading compare with his classmates' at the end of the silent period?
options: He finished last
He finished at the same time
He finished before any of them
He did not finish
HIGH.why: He finished his book before a single classmate had turned to the final page.

wrong.A: He did not finish last.
wrong.B: He finished earlier than the others.
wrong.D: He finished the entire book.

HIGH.stem: In the passage, the word "immersed" most nearly means —
options: completely tired out
gladly left behind
very angry at it
fully surrounded by
HIGH.why: The class spent the period fully immersed in silence, so they were surrounded by it.

wrong.A: Silence did not make him tired.
wrong.B: He finished first, so he was not left behind.
wrong.C: He was amazed, not angry.

HIGH.stem: Why did Faisal struggle to concentrate each day?
options: The noise made it hard to focus
His books were far too hard to read
He did not like his own teacher
He came to class late each day
HIGH.why: The room buzzed with talking, scraping chairs, and tapping pencils, and Faisal struggled to concentrate through all of it.

wrong.B: He read well once the room was quiet, so the books were not the problem.
wrong.C: The teacher is kind to him in the passage.
wrong.D: Being late is never mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What is the main job of the first paragraph?
options: To show exactly how the story ends
To teach readers how to read faster
To describe the noisy room and Faisal's problem
To introduce the teacher's new reading plan
HIGH.why: The first paragraph sets up the noisy classroom and Faisal's struggle before the teacher's plan appears.

wrong.A: The ending comes in the last paragraph.
wrong.B: The passage is not a how-to for fast reading.
wrong.D: The teacher's plan starts in the second paragraph.
